steps: Reverse anticoagulation urgently (vitamin K + PCC for warfarin; specific reversal agents for DOACs).
Lower SBP to ~140 mmHg (e.g. IV labetalol/nicardipine).
Manage raised ICP; neurosurgical referral (esp. cerebellar bleed, hydrocephalus).
Admit to stroke unit/ICU; VTE prophylaxis (mechanical first).

drugRefs.regimenLabel: IV beta/alpha-blocker for acute BP control
drugRefs.dose: 10-20 mg IV bolus, then infusion titrated to target
drugRefs.freq: repeat bolus every 10 min / infusion to SBP ~140 mmHg
drugRefs.why: Titratable agent to lower systolic BP towards ~140 mmHg and limit haematoma expansion.

drugRefs.dose: 5 mg/h, titrate by 2.5 mg/h every 5-15 min (max 15 mg/h)
drugRefs.why: Smoothly titratable BP control alternative to labetalol for the same target.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Intracerebral Haemorrhage
AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Haemorrhage
Neurocritical Care Society — Reversal of Antithrombotics in ICH

drugRefs.freq: single dose, guided by repeat INR
drugRefs.why: Rapid replacement of vitamin-K-dependent factors to reverse warfarin-associated ICH; faster than FFP.

drugRefs.regimenLabel: Vitamin K (with PCC for VKA reversal)
drugRefs.why: Given alongside PCC to sustain reversal of warfarin once the PCC effect wanes.
Specific reversal for dabigatran-associated haemorrhage; use factor-Xa-inhibitor reversal (e.g. andexanet/PCC) for apixaban/rivaroxaban.

refs: AHA/ASA Guideline for the Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Haemorrhage
Neurocritical Care Society — Reversal of Antithrombotics in ICH

decision.label: Reverse anticoagulation + lower SBP to ~140 mmHg

confirm: Sudden focal deficit ± reduced consciousness, headache, vomiting; non-contrast CT shows intraparenchymal haemorrhage.

investigations.test: CT angio if structural cause suspected
